title: Instant Pots and Swiss Cheese
html:
You know that sound an Instant Pot makes when it’s getting up to pressure? That unsettling hissing, spitting, gurgling sound?

That’s often how I feel.

Lots on my mind: graduate school, research, general upkeep… all the typical things.

They add up.

The hissing. Spurting. Gurgling. It seldom stops.

I need release valves — methods for decompressing and rejuvenating — lest I explode. Such release valves might also be called coping mechanisms, and we need several.

Coping shouldn’t, and likely can’t, be done entirely through a single mechanism. For the same reason that you don’t want to invest all your money in one asset, you don’t want to rely entirely on a single de-stressor. If it goes to zero, ie. you can’t access your cope, you’re SOL. So diversify, diversify, diversify. Through diversity, a robust set of coping mechanisms is like a stack of Swiss cheese slices. No slice is without its holes, but, with enough slices, all holes are covered.

My current stack keeps me (mostly) sane, and it consists of the following:

*We’ll leave aside psychological tools for now and focus on more embodied activities. Meditation and mental frames have been of immense value, but we’ll discuss those another time.*

  1. Weight Training — emotional regulation, discipline, resilience: Besides its obvious physical benefits, weight training functions as an emotional prophylactic AND therapeutic. In my experience, lifting weights in the morning grants me a negative emotion buffer. After I lift, I’m nearly un-botherable, and the emotional burdens I carried before the workout seem completely insubstantial. Also, adhering to training programs for weeks, months, and years on end develops your ability to do hard things more generally. See “In Defense of Masochism” for more on this.

  2. Jiu-Jitsu — community, socializing, play, silliness, physical expression: I made jiu-jitsu a non-negotiable in 2023. After I started training, I felt like everything was okay for the first time since moving away to college in 2020. The mats are a place for community, problem-solving, skill development, cultivating confidence and humility, athletic expression, playfulness, silliness, socializing, and physical contact. The mats are my happy place. So, for anyone considering jiu-jitsu, it has my unadulterated support.

  3. Playing Music — musical expression, creative expression, emotional expression: As someone who spends minimal time expressing their emotions to others (mainly due to my lifestyle as a graduate student and researcher, not because I’m a hermit by default), I express them through my instruments. How I bend a note on the guitar or strike a chord on the piano, is, in some sense, an externalization of my internal landscape. The converse relationship also exists, where the music I play, whether melancholy or uplifting, colors my mind. It lets me feel the feels that need feeling. In a very real way, music is therapy.

  4. Walks — processing time, time in nature: Walks declutter my mental inbox. Life presents us with an evergrowing queue of problems and pains that need handling, and walks (and sleep) work wonders to triage them. Without fail, every time I walk out the door with all that’s troubling me, I return with less.

  5. Writing — psychological decongestion, clarifying your thinking: Silly Substack posts like these give me a place to make explicit the amorphous concepts bumbling around in my head. I hypothesize that a non-trivial amount of the internal pressure I feel comes from how infrequently I get to brain vomit on my friends. I have lots to say, and, oftentimes, no one to say it to. So, I write. To quote a cultural icon: “Better out than in, I always say.” — Shrek

“Life is pain, Highness. Anyone who says differently is selling something.” — Wesley, The Princess Bride

In short, Wesley is right. Life is pain. And we can either let it consume us, or we can cope. Effective coping requires a diverse set of strategies that achieves complete coverage of our needs. With my cheese stack as inspiration, I encourage you to think about your own from first principles, find its holes, and determine how to cover them up.
